lessons.title: Nouns, plurals and articles
lessons.programRef: Form 1 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the main kinds of noun.
Form regular and common irregular plurals.
Choose a, an or the correctly.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: A **noun** names a person, place, thing, animal or idea. Every sentence about Cameroon is full of nouns: *Nana, Douala, a mango, hunger, the market*. Knowing the kind of noun helps you to choose capital letters, plurals and articles correctly.

blocks.title: Kinds of noun
blocks.md:
- **Common noun:** a general name (*girl, town, river*).
- **Proper noun:** the special name of one person or place; it begins with a **capital letter** (*Ngu, Buea, River Wouri*).
- **Abstract noun:** an idea or feeling we cannot touch (*joy, hunger, honesty*).
- **Collective noun:** a group (*a class, a team, a flock*).
- **Countable** nouns can be counted (*two eggs*); **uncountable** ones cannot (*rice, water, advice*).

blocks.caption: Ask: is it a general name, a special name, or an idea?
blocks.alt: A diagram with the word Noun at the top and three arrows to common (girl, town), proper (Buea, Ngu) and abstract (joy, hunger).

blocks.title: Plurals and articles
blocks.md:
- Most nouns add **-s**: *book, books*.
- After **s, x, ch, sh** add **-es**: *box, boxes; church, churches*.
- Consonant + **y** becomes **-ies**: *baby, babies*.
- Irregular: *man, men; child, children; woman, women; tooth, teeth; foot, feet*.
- Use **a** before a consonant **sound** (*a goat, a university*), **an** before a vowel sound (*an egg, an hour*), **the** for something already known (*the goat we bought*).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *Childrens, mans* are wrong: the plural of child is **children**.
- Uncountable nouns have no plural: say *some advice*, not *advices*; *some information*, not *informations*.
- Do not forget capital letters for proper nouns: *Bamenda*, not *bamenda*.
- Choose a / an by the **sound**, not the spelling: *an honest man, a European*.

blocks.title: Example 1: a plural
steps: *church* ends in **ch**, so add **-es**: *churches*.
*baby* is consonant + y: change y to **ies**: *babies*.
*child* is irregular: *children*.

blocks.title: Example 2: a or an?
blocks.statement: Complete: *I bought ___ orange and ___ pineapple at the market.*
steps: *orange* starts with a vowel sound, so use **an**.
*pineapple* starts with a consonant sound, so use **a**.

lessons.title: Pronouns and words that point to nouns
lessons.programRef: Form 1 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use subject, object and possessive pronouns correctly.
Use this, that, these and those.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: A **pronoun** takes the place of a noun so that we do not repeat it. Compare: *Ngum took Ngum's bag and Ngum went home* with *Ngum took his bag and he went home*. Pronouns change their form depending on their job in the sentence.

blocks.title: Pronoun forms
blocks.md:
- **Subject:** I, you, he, she, it, we, they (they do the action).
- **Object:** me, you, him, her, it, us, them (they receive the action).
- **Possessive adjective** (before a noun): my, your, his, her, its, our, their.
- **Possessive pronoun** (alone): mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.
*She gave me her book. The book is hers.*

blocks.title: Pointing words
blocks.md: **This / these** point to things that are **near**; **that / those** point to things that are **far**. *This mango (in my hand) is sweet; that mango (on the tree) is not ripe.* **This** and **that** are singular, **these** and **those** are plural.

blocks.caption: The same person, three forms.
blocks.alt: A table with three columns, subject, object and possessive, listing I me my mine, he him his, she her hers, we us ours and they them theirs.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *Me and Ada went to school* is wrong: use **Ada and I went** (subject). After a verb or preposition use the object form: *She gave it to Ada and me.*
- *It's* means *it is*; **its** shows ownership (*the dog wagged its tail*).
- *Their* (belonging to them), *there* (place), *they're* (they are) are different words.

blocks.title: Example 1: subject or object?
blocks.statement: Choose the right word: *Mama called Ada and (I / me) to the kitchen.*
steps: *Ada and ___* are the **objects** of called (Mama did the calling).
Take Ada away: *Mama called me.* So the correct word is **me**.

blocks.title: Example 2: replace the nouns
blocks.statement: Rewrite using pronouns: *Nkem lost Nkem's pen, so Nkem asked Tabi and Tabi's sister to look for the pen.*
steps: Replace repeated names: Nkem becomes **he or she**, Nkem's becomes **his or her**.
*Tabi and Tabi's sister* becomes **them**, and *the pen* becomes **it**.
blocks.answer: Nkem lost her pen, so she asked them to look for it.

lessons.title: Present simple and present continuous
lessons.programRef: Form 1 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use the present simple for habits and facts.
Use the present continuous for actions happening now.
Make the verb agree with its subject (he/she/it + s).
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: We use the **present simple** for things that are always true or happen regularly, and the **present continuous** for things happening **now** or around now. *Kumba sells fish every Monday* (habit). *She is selling fish at this moment* (now).

blocks.title: Present simple
blocks.md:
Use the base verb; add **-s / -es** after *he, she, it* and singular nouns.
- *I walk to school. Mary walks to school.*
- **Questions and negatives** use **do / does**: *Does she walk? She does not walk.* After *does* the verb has **no -s**.
- Signal words: *always, usually, every day, often, never, on Sundays.*

blocks.title: Present continuous
blocks.md:
Form: **am / is / are + verb-ing**. *I am reading. He is cooking. They are playing.* Questions: *Are they playing?* Negative: *He is not cooking.*
Signal words: *now, at the moment, today, these days, look!*
Stative verbs (*know, like, want, understand*) are normally **not** used in the continuous: say *I know the answer*, not *I am knowing*.

blocks.caption: Habit or action in progress? Choose the tense by the meaning.
blocks.alt: A table comparing the present simple, used for habits and facts, for example She sells fish, with the present continuous, used for actions happening now, for example She is selling.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *He go to school* → **He goes** to school (add -es).
- *Does she goes?* → **Does she go?** (no -s after does).
- *I am know* → **I know** (stative verb).
- *She is cook now* → **She is cooking** (do not forget -ing).
- Spelling: *run → running, make → making, study → studying*.

blocks.title: Example 1: choose the tense
blocks.statement: Complete: *Every morning Ngwa (wash / is washing) his face, but look! He (wash / is washing) the car now.*
steps: *Every morning* shows a habit: present simple, **washes**.
*Look!* and *now* show an action in progress: **is washing**.

blocks.title: Example 2: make a question
blocks.statement: Turn into a question: *Tabi plays football on Saturdays.*
steps: The verb is in the present simple, so we use **does** (Tabi = he).
After *does* the main verb loses its -s: *Does Tabi play football on Saturdays?*
blocks.answer: Does Tabi play football on Saturdays?

lessons.title: The simple past tense
lessons.programRef: Form 1 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Form the simple past of regular and irregular verbs.
Make past questions and negatives with did.
Use time expressions such as yesterday and last year.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: The **simple past** tells us about actions that finished at a definite time before now: *Yesterday we visited my grandfather in Bafoussam. We ate achu and returned in the evening.*

blocks.title: Forming the simple past
blocks.md:
- **Regular verbs** add **-ed**: *walk → walked; play → played*. If the verb ends in e add **-d** (*live → lived*); consonant + y becomes **-ied** (*carry → carried*).
- **Irregular verbs** change form: *go → went, eat → ate, see → saw, buy → bought, come → came, write → wrote, have → had, bring → brought*.
- Time words: *yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago.*

blocks.title: Questions and negatives
blocks.md:
Use **did** (for every subject) and the **base verb**:
- *Did you go to the match? No, I did not (didn't) go.*
- *She did not buy any fish.*
The past form shows only **once**: *did + go*, never *did + went*.

items.text: Question or negative: did + base verb

blocks.caption: Four quick decisions.
blocks.alt: A flowchart of four boxes: is the action finished, regular verb add ed, irregular verb learn the form, and question or negative use did plus the base verb.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *Did he went?* → **Did he go?**
- *I buyed a dress* → **I bought** a dress.
- *She didn't saw me* → **She didn't see me.**
- Do not mix tenses in one story: if you begin with *went*, continue with *saw, bought, came*.
- Spelling: *stop → stopped, plan → planned*.

blocks.title: Example 1: put in the past
blocks.statement: Rewrite in the past: *Ada goes to Limbe and buys fish.*
steps: Add a time word: *Last Sunday*.
*goes → went, buys → bought*.
blocks.answer: Last Sunday Ada went to Limbe and bought fish.

blocks.title: Example 2: negative
steps: Use **did not** and the base form: *watch*.
Do not keep the -ed: *did not watched* is wrong.
blocks.answer: They did not watch the match.

lessons.title: Adjectives, adverbs and comparison
lessons.programRef: Form 1 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: An **adjective** describes a noun (*a heavy bag, the red soil*). An **adverb** describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb and often answers *how, when, where*: *She walked slowly. He arrived early.* Many adverbs of manner end in **-ly**.

blocks.title: Comparing things
blocks.md:
- Short adjectives: **-er / -est**: *tall, taller, tallest*; *big, bigger, biggest*; *happy, happier, happiest*.
- Long adjectives: **more / most**: *beautiful, more beautiful, the most beautiful*.
- Irregular: *good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; far, farther, farthest*.
Use **than** to compare two things: *Mount Cameroon is higher than the hill near our school.*

blocks.title: Making adverbs
blocks.md: Add **-ly** to an adjective: *quick → quickly; careful → carefully; happy → happily*. Some adverbs keep the same form: *fast, hard, late, early*. **Good** is an adjective, **well** is an adverb: *She is a good singer. She sings well.*

blocks.caption: Learn the irregular rows by heart.
blocks.alt: A table with base, comparative and superlative forms: tall taller tallest, good better best, bad worse worst, important more important most important.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *more taller, most best* (double comparison) → **taller**, **best**.
- *He runs quick* → **He runs quickly.**
- *She speaks good English* → **She speaks English well** (or *good English* as a noun phrase: *She has good English*).
- *Ada is more tall than Ngu* → **taller than**.
- Use **than**, not *then*, after a comparative.

blocks.title: Example 1: comparative
blocks.statement: Complete: *This plantain is ___ (big) than that one, but the pineapple is the ___ (heavy) fruit in the basket.*
steps: Comparing two things: *big → bigger* (double the g).
Comparing many: *heavy → the heaviest* (y becomes i).

blocks.title: Example 2: adjective or adverb?
blocks.statement: Choose: *The students listened (careful / carefully) to the careful (teacher / teaching).*
steps: *listened* is a verb, so we need an adverb: **carefully**.
*careful* is an adjective describing a noun.

lessons.title: Prepositions and linking words
lessons.programRef: Form 1 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use prepositions of place, time and movement.
Join short sentences with and, but, or, so and because.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: A **preposition** shows the relation between a noun or pronoun and another word: *The book is **on** the table. We arrive **at** noon.* A **conjunction** joins words or sentences: *I like rice **and** beans, **but** I do not like okra.*

blocks.title: Common prepositions
blocks.md:
- **Place:** *in* (inside a space: *in the room, in Douala*), *on* (a surface: *on the desk*), *at* (a point: *at the gate, at school*), *under, behind, between, beside, near.*
- **Time:** *at* (clock times: *at six o'clock*), *on* (days and dates: *on Monday, on 11 February*), *in* (months, years, parts of the day: *in May, in 2024, in the morning*).
- **Movement:** *to, from, into, across, through, along, up, down.*

blocks.title: Linking words
blocks.md:
- **and** adds an idea; **but** shows contrast; **or** gives a choice; **so** gives a result; **because** gives a reason.
*I was hungry, so I bought puff-puff.* / *I bought puff-puff because I was hungry.*
Put a comma before *but, so* when they join two full clauses.

blocks.caption: At = a point, on = a day, in = a longer period.
blocks.alt: A table of time prepositions: at with six o'clock, noon and night; on with Monday, my birthday and Friday morning; in with May, 2024 and the evening.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *I will meet you in Monday* → **on** Monday.
- *She is good in English* → **good at** English.
- *He is afraid from dogs* → **afraid of** dogs.
- *We discussed about the problem* → **discussed the problem** (no about).
- Do not write *because* and *so* together: *Because it rained, so we stayed home* → choose one.

blocks.title: Example 1: choose the preposition
blocks.statement: Fill in at, on or in: *The match starts ___ Saturday ___ 3 p.m. ___ Buea.*
steps: A day takes **on**: *on Saturday*.
A clock time takes **at**: *at 3 p.m.*; a town takes **in**: *in Buea*.
blocks.answer: on Saturday at 3 p.m. in Buea

blocks.title: Example 2: join with a linking word
blocks.statement: Join with *so*: *The road was flooded. We took another way.*
steps: *so* gives a **result**: the flooding is the cause.
Put a comma before so: *The road was flooded, so we took another way.*
blocks.answer: The road was flooded, so we took another way.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Write a short note (4–5 sentences) telling a friend about a plan for next Saturday. Use at least three prepositions and the linking words *but* and *because*.
exercises.model: On Saturday I will go to the farm with my uncle. We will leave at six o'clock in the morning. I want to go because I like picking oranges. I would stay longer, but I must return before dark.
rubric: 1 mark: three prepositions used correctly.
1 mark: *but* used correctly.
1 mark: *because* used correctly.
1 mark: clear meaning and punctuation.
exercises.explanation: On Saturday I will go to the farm with my uncle. We will leave at six o'clock in the morning. I want to go because I like picking oranges. I would stay longer, but I must return before dark.
